newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end higher on weather jitters.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end higher on weather jitters.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended a choppy session higher on Wednesday, lifted by uncertainties about the weather and persistent talk that China was looking to buy U.S. soybeans, traders said.

"We had some speculative selling in new crop based on what appears to be some good weather but it ran into some commercial buying late and that pushed it higher," said Bob Lekberg, analyst with Goldenberg-Hehmeyer. "There's continued talk of ongoing Chinese interest in both U.S. soybeans and soybean meal."
Weather forecasts gave conflicting views, traders said.
Meteorologists predicted a hot, dry spell this weekend for the U.S. Midwest but said the heat wave would be short lived as a cold front pushed through late Sunday into Monday.

Some midday updates suggested heavier rainfall amounts next week while others indicated lighter coverage. While August is seen as the critical month for soybean development, extremely hot, dry weather in July can stress soybean crops.
There were some scattered reports of wind and hail damage overnight in western Iowa, traders said.
Soybeans ended 3-3/4 to 1-3/4 cents per bushel higher with August up 3-3/4 at $7.39.
Talk continued to circulate that China was looking to buy new crop soybeans. Hong Kong traders said Chinese buyers were very interested in new crop U.S. soybeans and were likely making enquiries.
But with huge arrivals of soybeans and meal expected in the second half of the year, traders said they were cautious over actual deals concluded at this stage.
Nearbys struggled with heavy deliveries posted against the July but traders noted commercials were the primary stoppers of the 1.930 million bushels posted.

Technical indicators were also said to be bullish for November. Traders said that contract took out the 10-day moving average at $6.06 which prompted some fund buying interest. Prices subsided near midday as traders awaited midday weather updates, pit sources said.
On the day, Merrill Lynch and USA Trading each bought two million bushels November and Lee B. Stern sold two million November, pit sources said.

Spread trade was said to be active with commercials the larges players. Produce Grain spread 2.4 million bushels September/November at 42-1/2 to 44 cents, premium September, and Central Soya spread one million November/August at $1.30, premium August.
In options, Tenco Inc bought 400 November $6.25 calls at 21-3/4 to 24 cents and ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp sold 400 November $6.00 puts at 25 cents.
Volatility in the November was at 23-1/2 percent, down from Tuesday's 24 percent.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 40,000 contracts, against Tuesday's actual volume of 39,203. Options volume was pegged at 18,000 contracts, against Tuesday's 10,115 contracts.
